title: The Man Who Kept Books
subtitle: Detroit, Pontiac and Chicago
focus: The Detroit revue and its uncredited house bands, techno as the next branch, and Chicago: electric blues, gospel quartets, steppers and house music born in the warehouse

intro.t: Detroit at dusk. The river on one side, Canada across it, and the city's lights coming on one at a time, like a band nobody bothered to introduce.
This town made a thousand records with the same players in the basement and never said who they were. Nobody announced me either. We have that in common.
Inventory, for the record. Gloves on. Item one: one reel box, grey cloth, Nana's handwriting. Item two: one pencil rubbing, dead wax, five letters.
Item three: one lead. Quote: 'Low kept a little book. Detroit boy.' End quote.
That ain't a lead. That's a fortune cookie.
It's a bass player who wrote things down. Do you know how rare that is? Fun fact - most session players in the sixties never even -
Where do bass players go in Detroit?
Same place as everybody who never got introduced, Pocket. The basement. And tonight the basement's playing the revue.

outro.t: The van points south. Tuesday has the ledger open on her knees to the address page, as if it might change its mind.
Ruth, Memphis. Wendell, New Orleans. The Professor, overseas. That's a river and an ocean.
River first. The Choir don't swim.
Harlem made me. The Bronx played me twice at the same time. Philly dressed me up in strings. D.C. would not let me end.
Detroit forgot to introduce me. Chicago put me on the floor and made me dance till morning. Every one of them remembered me. Not one of them remembered who.

gigs.title: Revue Night
gigs.blurb: A revue with a house band that has backed every act for thirty years and never once been introduced.

challenge.text: Introduce the band: play this set with at least 2 people.

before.t: The Motor City Grand. Gold leaf to the ceiling, a balcony that leans over the stage like it wants to hear better, and revue night: eight acts, one band.
Act after act walks out to the lip of the stage in a new suit. Behind every one of them, in the same seats, in the same jackets: the Basement Saints.
Velvet Odom, master of ceremonies. Let me see my card. Next up... the Mt. Nebo Youth Choir. Beautiful. What hymn are we doing, children?
It's a van. Somebody tell him it's a van.
Mr. Odom, the choir is the van. The band is the band.
Brother, I have introduced stranger things than a van.
In the corner, Hollis Gaines is tuning between acts the way he has for longer than you have been alive. BASEMENT SAINTS on his jacket, in thread gone gold with age.
How long have you been the house band?
Fifty years. Nobody ever asked our names.
Mr. Odom. Tonight, will you introduce the band? By name. All of them.
Introduce the band. Fifty years and nobody asked me that either.
Tell you what, children. If that balcony stands up for you, I'll do it.
Ladies and gentlemen, the Mt. Nebo... I'm being told that is a van.
Ladies and gentlemen... {band}!

afterWin.t: The balcony stands. All of it. The old gold leaf seems to lean in.
Well. A deal is a deal. Ladies and gentlemen, before you go home tonight... the band.
On the drums, Mr. Raymond Dukes.
The balcony stands for him. Raymond Dukes stands up too, by accident, and sits back down like he got caught.
On the keys, Miss Sylvia Pruett. On the horns, the Barnes brothers, Cleophus and June. On guitar, Mr. Earl Witcher, who has never once been late.
The balcony does not sit down between names. It has decided not to.
And on bass, leading the Basement Saints for fifty years... Mr. Hollis Gaines.
I have been announced on ten thousand records. Never once like that.
Fifty years. Fifty years, and it took a youth choir.
We're looking for a bass player called Low. He kept a little book.
Low Castile. Lord. Gone a long time now. His daughter owns the Pontiac Ballroom. Plays his bass.
Don't call it the bass in front of her. Call it his.

afterLose.t: Basement's always open. Come on back down.
Fifty years he's been waiting on a name. He can wait one more set. Run it back.

gigs.title: His Left Hand's Daughter
gigs.blurb: Ren Castile owns the room, plays her father's bass, and is not in the business of making strangers feel better.

challenge.text: Low never dropped a note in his life. Play one song with no misses.

before.t: The Pontiac Ballroom. A sprung wooden floor, a bar older than most of its customers, and one light over the stage that flickers like it's thinking it over.
Up a ladder, fixing that light: a woman in coveralls and a bandana, a ring of club keys on her belt, and a bass slung across her back.
If you're the electrician, you're late. If you're not the electrician, you're in my light.
Ms. Castile? This is going to sound strange. We think your father played on a record in 1967.
My father played on a lot of records. Most of them didn't say so.
My father died owed. I'm not in the business of making strangers feel better about that.
Hollis said to call it his.
Hollis talks too much. He's right, though.
I'm not him. I'm his left hand's daughter.
She comes down the ladder, wipes her hands, and looks out the front window at the van. She reads the side of it. Slowly. Under her breath.
Mt. Nebo Youth Choir.
Something happens to her face that she has clearly not authorized.
Fine. You made me laugh, and that's rarer than an electrician who shows up. You get one night. The room decides the rest.
Yes, ma'am.

afterWin.t: Ren wipes down his strings with a rag from her back pocket, slow, before she says a word. Then she goes into the office and comes back with something small.
He wrote everything down. Every session, every studio, every dollar. Like if he wrote it, somebody would have to pay it.
A pocket ledger, black oilcloth, the corners worn round. Tuesday has her gloves on before anybody asks.
December thirty-first, sixty-seven. 'Lantern, back room. Watch Night. Fifteen dollars, plus plate.'
And under it: 'D. got paper. We got a plate.'
What does that mean?
I've read that line my whole life. Never could make it say anything.
Somebody just turned the bass up in me.
Take it. Bring it back with his name on something.
Ms. Castile, may I film the page and post it? Somebody out there might know what it means.
You asked. Most people don't. Yes.

afterLose.t: He used to say the first set's for the band. Second set's for the room. Go again.
She doesn't leave the light on for just anybody. Run it back.

gigs.title: For the Room Only
gigs.blurb: Lantern's lawyers have written to the theater. Miss Tempo has a basket for your phones.

challenge.text: For the room only: earn 12 stars for the people who put their phones in the basket.

before.t: It's gone. The ledger video. It had people guessing all night, and at seven this morning: 'removed following a legal complaint.'
Complaint from who?
Lantern Legacy's lawyers. On behalf of, quote, the rights holder.
The South Side Regal. The manager meets you at the stage door holding a letter on cream paper with a gold lantern at the top. I am starting to recognize the stationery.
It reminds the theater, very politely, of the risks of 'hosting the unauthorized exhibition of recordings'. The manager looks ready to cancel you, very politely.
Sugar, give me that.
Miss Tempo. House DJ since the warehouse days. Silver sneakers, a towel over one shoulder, and a laundry basket on her hip.
Phones. All of them. In the basket. Yours too, sugar. Yours especially.
That's my whole archive.
Then you'll remember tonight the old way. With your feet.
They can take a video down. They can't take a room down.
What if somebody films anyway?
Then they'll be the only one in here not dancing, and everybody will know. Sugar, I've been running this floor since before the floor had a name.
By eight the basket is full and the floor is fuller. Nobody is filming. Everybody is here. Four on the floor. One, two, three, four.

afterWin.t: Two in the morning, under the marquee. The bulbs are still warm. Miss Tempo hands back the phones one at a time, like a coat check.
Cousin. There's an address page in the back of the ledger. In his hand.
'Sister (Ruth) - Memphis, Beale, Saturdays.'
'Deacon (Wendell) - New Orleans, the brass band.'
'Professor (A.) - overseas, 1969.'
Ruth. Wendell. A.
Three of the five who made me just got first names. Well. Two names and an initial. I am counting the initial.
And much later in the book, in a different pen: '1984. Called Mr. Lark. Nothing.'
Nobody says anything for a while. The bulbs tick as they cool.
Memphis. New Orleans. That's straight down the river, Pocket.
I got a cousin in Memphis.
Is there a city where you don't?

afterLose.t: Sugar, the floor's still here. Again.
Nobody filmed that one. Lucky you. Run it back.

afterChallenge.t: Watch Night, 1967. Ten minutes past midnight. The church let out onto the steps, and it had started, lightly, to snow.
The guitar player told Mother Clementine she had never heard that hymn sung that way, and she wanted to learn it before she forgot it.
Mother Clementine opened her hymnal to 211 and tore the page out, neatly, right there on the church steps. Nobody said one word to her about it.
In the margin, in her own pencil, years old already: 'sing it C.F.'s way'.
The bass player asked what the date was. Somebody told him it was a brand-new year, ten minutes old. He wrote it down anyway, in the little book.
The guitar player had no case. She carried her guitar wrapped in a pillowcase, and nobody asked where the pillowcase came from.
The organist said he knew a back door two blocks over, at Lantern Records, and that the man upstairs was throwing a party.
Five of them walked there through the snow. Not one of them knew they were on their way to make me. That's the best way to be made.
